analysis.one_liner: Lets governors block endangered species listings and pays landowners when protections lower property values.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: Senator Rand Paul introduced it with zero cosponsors, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Endangered Species Act so that no species could be listed as endangered or threatened without the consent of every governor in states where it lives, and no listing would take effect until both chambers of Congress pass a joint resolution approving it. Every listing would expire automatically after five years. A governor could take over regulation of any species found only within that state, and those decisions could not be challenged in court. Landowners could get a ruling on whether a planned use of their property is allowed — and if the Interior Department doesn't answer within 90 days, it counts as a yes. If the government says no, the landowner could demand payment of 150% of the property's value. The bill would also strip attorney-fee awards in endangered-species lawsuits, and lift protections for black vultures and ravens that damage livestock or property.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and lessees of land where endangered or threatened species live — including developers, ranchers, and timber and energy interests — gain the most. They would get a fast-track property-use ruling with an automatic approval if the agency misses the deadline, cash compensation of 150% of fair market value when a listing or agency decision cuts into their property's use, and far fewer listings to contend with because any one governor in a species' range could veto it and Congress would have to affirmatively approve every list. Public power customers would see the cost of species compliance itemized on their monthly electric bills, a disclosure aimed at building pressure against the law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners, developers, ranchers, and timber and energy interests

how_it_helps.text: The Interior Department would have to answer a landowner's property-use application within 90 days; if it doesn't, the proposed use is deemed not to violate the Endangered Species Act, and the landowner can rely on that as a legal defense [S3].

If an agency action reduces the intended-use value of property by at least 50%, the owner or lessee can be paid 150% of its fair market value within 180 days, with the government covering appraisal costs [S3].

No species could be listed without the consent of the governor of each state where it is present, and no listing would take effect until Congress enacts a joint resolution approving it; all listed species would be removed from the list five years later unless Congress votes to relist them [S2][S3].

A governor could claim exclusive authority to manage any species found only within that state — including on federal public lands — and those decisions would be exempt from judicial review in any court [S3].
Attorney-fee awards in endangered-species citizen suits would be eliminated, removing a key funding mechanism conservation groups use to enforce the law [S2][S3].

The bill would allow people to kill black vultures they believe threaten livestock, vehicles, or buildings, and allow raven population control where state wildlife agencies find ravens threaten recovery of listed or candidate species [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the 150% property-value compensation payments and appraisal costs. The public would pay with weakened species protection: listings would be far rarer and shorter-lived, and state takeovers of intrastate species could not be reviewed by any court. Federal power marketing administrations would have to itemize species-compliance costs on customers' electric bills, which does not itself raise rates but makes visible — and politically targetable — the cost of protecting species such as salmon that affect dam operations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, and the public losing species protections

drawbacks.text: The combination of a gubernatorial veto, mandatory congressional approval, and a five-year sunset would make new species listings extremely rare, effectively hollowing out the Endangered Species Act while keeping it on the books [S2][S3].
Exempting state governors' species-management decisions from judicial review means a state could manage a species to extinction with no court able to stop it [S3].

Paying landowners 150% of fair market value whenever an agency action halves a property's intended-use value, and deeming every unanswered application approved after 90 days, would create large federal liabilities and a built-in route around habitat protections [S3].

A good-faith supporter's case: the Act does impose real costs on landowners who bear conservation burdens for a national public good, and the bill's compensation and cost-accounting provisions attempt to shift some of that burden back to taxpayers as a whole [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow narrowly to landowners and resource industries, while the costs are broad: a much-weakened national safety net for imperiled species, expensive compensation liabilities for taxpayers, and no judicial check on state management. Even the bill's transparency provisions, like itemizing compliance costs on electric bills, are designed more to build a case against the Act than to protect anyone. Weighed honestly, the costs to conservation and the public treasury outweigh what landowners would gain, though the underlying complaint — that individual landowners shoulder costs for a public good — is a real policy problem that could be addressed more narrowly.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Paul introduced it in March 2021 and it was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it; when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, the bill died.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the Endangered Species Management Self-Determination Act on March 10, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party [S4].
The committee held no markup, reported no bill, and the Senate never voted on it; the bill expired at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, existing Endangered Species Act protections — automatic listings based on science, citizen suits with attorney fees, and federal authority over all species — remained in place. Landowners and industries hoping for compensation payments, state takeovers, and 90-day automatic approvals did not get them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Endangered species protections; the bill's backers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 10, 2021, and recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup, reported the bill out, or scheduled any action; the bill sat for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded.

industries.industry: Property owners and real estate developers
industries.note: The bill would hand landowners 150%-of-value compensation when species protections cut into their property's use, plus an automatic approval if the Interior Department misses a 90-day deadline on any proposed use. Their gain comes directly out of habitat protection, a public good.

The bill would let people kill black vultures believed to be threatening livestock, vehicles, or buildings, and allow raven control where ravens threaten recovery of listed species. This addresses a real property-damage problem, but at the cost of migratory-bird protections.

These groups would lose attorney-fee awards in citizen suits — their main enforcement tool — and face a system where any governor in a species' range and a congressional vote both stand between a species and protection. Their interest tracks with the public interest in species survival.

industries.industry: Federal power marketing administrations and their electric customers
industries.note: The bill would require the Bonneville, Southeastern, Southwestern, and Western Area power administrations to itemize the cost of Endangered Species Act compliance on every customer's monthly bill. This is disclosure, not a rate change, but it spotlights the cost of species protection on customers — such as costs tied to salmon protection at federal dams — to build pressure for weaker rules.
